name: United Kingdom
summary: UK banks are dual-regulated: the PRA (part of the Bank of England) supervises safety and soundness and operational resilience, while the FCA sets conduct, financial crime and consumer rules and supervises compliance with the Money Laundering Regulations. OFSI (HM Treasury) runs financial sanctions, the NCA receives suspicious activity reports, the ICO enforces data protection, HMRC oversees FATCA/CRS reporting and the Financial Ombudsman Service resolves complaints. Training duties are a mix of express statutory or Handbook obligations (AML/CTF training under MLR regulation 24, Conduct Rules training under COCON, whistleblowing training under SYSC 18, role qualifications under TC, health and safety) and broader competence expectations (SYSC 5 competent employees rule, Consumer Duty, operational resilience, failure-to-prevent offences).

regulators.name: Financial Conduct Authority
regulators.role: Conduct regulator for all banks; sets the FCA Handbook (SYSC, COCON, TC, PRIN 2A Consumer Duty, DISP, CONC) and supervises banks for the Money Laundering Regulations.

regulators.name: Prudential Regulation Authority (Bank of England)
regulators.role: Prudential supervisor of deposit-takers; co-owner of the Senior Managers and Certification Regime and of operational resilience, outsourcing and incident reporting rules.

regulators.name: Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (HM Treasury)
regulators.role: Implements and enforces UK financial sanctions; receives breach and frozen-asset reports from relevant firms, including banks.

regulators.name: HM Revenue & Customs
regulators.role: Receives FATCA and CRS reports from UK financial institutions under the International Tax Compliance Regulations.

regulators.name: Information Commissioner's Office
regulators.role: Enforces UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018 and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, including breach notification and the new complaints duty.

regulators.name: National Crime Agency (UK Financial Intelligence Unit)
regulators.role: Receives suspicious activity reports (SARs) and defence-against-money-laundering requests under POCA and the Terrorism Act.

regulators.name: Financial Ombudsman Service
regulators.role: Independent statutory body that resolves complaints from eligible customers that banks have not settled under DISP.

regulators.name: Payment Systems Regulator
regulators.role: Runs the APP scam reimbursement requirement for Faster Payments; being consolidated into the FCA.

programs.title: United Kingdom | MLR 2017 Regulation 24 AML Awareness Training
programs.why: Regulation 24 of the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 obliges every relevant person, including banks, to make relevant employees, and since January 2020 any agents doing comparable work, aware of the law on money laundering, terrorist financing and (since September 2022) proliferation financing and of the related data protection requirements, to train them regularly, and to keep a written record. The FCA's Financial Crime Guide treats role-specific training before staff deal with customers as good practice. POCA s.330 also gives untrained staff a limited defence, so missing training weakens the bank's control environment.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Current text: relevant employees and agents doing similar work must be made aware of ML, TF and PF law and data protection requirements and be trained regularly to recognise and handle suspicious activity; a written record of measures and training is required. Agents added from 10 January 2020 (SI 2019/1511), PF from 1 September 2022 (SI 2022/860).

references.title: The Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Regulations 2026
references.note: Targeted amendments to the 2017 Regulations, mostly in force 30 June 2026 (regulation 34A from 1 February 2027, some cryptoasset change-of-control rules from 25 October 2027). It does not amend regulation 24, so the training duty is unchanged.

references.title: FCG 2 Financial crime systems and controls
references.note: Guidance asking whether staff are aware of financial crime risks, whether training is tailored to roles and kept current, and how effectiveness is assessed.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Counter-Terrorist Financing Training (MLR 2017)
programs.why: The regulation 24 training duty covers terrorist financing as well as money laundering, so staff must understand the terrorist financing offences and how to spot and escalate related activity. Banks also face disclosure duties for terrorist property, so the training needs to explain the UK reporting route through the nominated officer to the NCA.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: The awareness and regular-training duty expressly covers terrorist financing law and recognising and handling activity that may be linked to it.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Proliferation Financing Risk (MLR Regulations 18A and 19A)
programs.why: Since 1 September 2022 regulation 24 has expressly required banks to make relevant employees aware of proliferation financing law and to train them regularly to recognise and deal with activity that may be linked to proliferation financing. Banks must also identify and assess proliferation financing risk (regulation 18A) and mitigate it through policies and controls (regulation 19A). PF content therefore belongs in the regular AML/CTF training, with deeper coverage for staff who run these controls.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: The awareness and regular-training duty names proliferation financing alongside money laundering and terrorist financing.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Regulations 18A and 19A require a PF risk assessment and matching policies and controls; regulation 21 screening and internal-control duties cover PF risk for relevant employees.

references.title: FCG 7 Sanctions, asset freezes and proliferation financing
references.note: FCA guidance on sanctions and proliferation financing systems and controls.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Customer Due Diligence under the MLR 2017
programs.why: CDD duties in Part 3 of the Money Laundering Regulations are part of the anti-money laundering law that regulation 24 says relevant employees must be made aware of. Staff who open accounts or service customers must know when CDD applies, what identification and verification is needed and what to do when it cannot be completed.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.provision: Part 3 (customer due diligence, regulations 27 to 38) read with regulation 24
references.note: Sets the CDD measures; regulation 24 requires staff to be made aware of these legal requirements and trained regularly.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Enhanced Due Diligence (MLR Regulation 33)
programs.why: The Regulations list situations that require enhanced due diligence, including business with persons established in a country on the FATF list of high-risk jurisdictions subject to a call for action (since 30 June 2026 this replaced the earlier high-risk third country test) and unusually complex or unusually large transactions. Staff applying EDD need the skills that regulation 21 screening tests, but no stand-alone EDD course is prescribed.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Sets out when enhanced due diligence and enhanced ongoing monitoring must be applied; as amended from 30 June 2026 it refers to FATF call-for-action countries.

references.title: The Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Regulations 2026
references.note: Replaced 'high-risk third country' with 'FATF call for action country' in regulation 33 and narrowed the complex-transaction trigger, from 30 June 2026. Its new regulation 34A (from 1 February 2027) applies only to cryptoasset exchange and custodian wallet providers.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Ongoing Monitoring of Business Relationships (MLR 2017)
programs.why: Banks must keep monitoring business relationships, scrutinising transactions and keeping CDD information up to date. Staff carrying out periodic reviews and trigger-event refreshes need to know these duties; the regulation 24 training duty covers recognising suspicious activity but the Regulations do not prescribe a separate course on ongoing monitoring.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Requires ongoing monitoring of business relationships, including scrutiny of transactions and keeping due diligence documents and information up to date.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Beneficial Ownership Identification (MLR 2017)
programs.why: For corporate and trust customers, banks must identify beneficial owners, take reasonable measures to verify them and understand ownership and control, and report material discrepancies with the Companies House register. Staff handling entity customers need this knowledge to meet the competence and screening expectations, though no separate course is mandated.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Sets beneficial ownership identification and reasonable verification duties within CDD, and the duty to report material discrepancies in the companies register.

programs.title: United Kingdom | PEPs: FCA Guidance FG17/6 and FG25/3
programs.why: The Regulations require EDD for politically exposed persons, and since 10 January 2024 a domestic PEP (or family member or close associate) starts from a lower risk assessment than a foreign PEP. The FCA's 2024 review found every assessed firm needed to improve, including most firms' staff training, and it issued revised guidance (FG25/3) in 2025. Staff must apply the right level of scrutiny without over-treating UK PEPs and their families.

references.title: FG17/6: The treatment of politically exposed persons for anti-money laundering purposes
references.note: The original 2017 FCA guidance on proportionate treatment of PEPs, family members and close associates, since revised by FG25/3.

references.title: The treatment of politically exposed persons for anti-money laundering purposes (FG25/3)
references.note: Revised FCA PEP guidance (July 2025) following the domestic PEP review, reflecting the lower-risk starting point for UK PEPs and changes to senior management sign-off.

references.title: The treatment of politically exposed persons (multi-firm review)
references.note: All assessed firms needed to improve; some used PEP definitions wider than the law or lacked declassification checks, and most needed better staff training.

programs.title: United Kingdom | OFSI Financial Sanctions Compliance
programs.why: UK sanctions regulations made under the Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 prohibit dealing with designated persons and require relevant firms, which include banks, to report knowledge or suspicion to OFSI. No statute prescribes sanctions training, but the FCA expects effective sanctions systems and controls, and OFSI's 2026 Bank of Scotland penalty commentary stresses regularly reviewed and updated sanctions training.

references.title: UK financial sanctions general guidance
references.note: Explains prohibitions, licensing and the duty of relevant firms, including their staff, to report knowledge or suspicion of designated persons or breaches to OFSI.

references.title: Sanctions compliance in practice: lessons from OFSI's £160,000 Bank of Scotland penalty
references.note: Links screening, escalation and training weaknesses to breach risk and calls for regular review of sanctions training.

references.title: FCG 7 Sanctions, asset freezes and proliferation financing
references.note: FCA guidance on governance, screening and staff awareness for sanctions.

programs.title: United Kingdom | US OFAC Awareness for UK Banks
programs.why: OFAC rules are not UK law, but UK banks clearing US dollars or with US nexus routinely apply them. Awareness of how US secondary sanctions risk differs from the UK regime is good practice; no UK obligation to train on OFAC was verified.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Suspicious Activity Reporting to the NCA (POCA and MLR)
programs.why: Regulation 24 requires regular training on how to recognise and deal with transactions and activity that may be linked to money laundering or terrorist financing. Under POCA s.330, staff in the regulated sector commit an offence by failing to report knowledge or suspicion; an employee who did not actually suspect and was not given the specified training has a defence, which shows the law expects banks to train staff on internal reporting and SARs.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Regular training on identifying and dealing with suspicious transactions is expressly required.

references.title: Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 - Explanatory Notes (section 330)
references.note: Failure-to-disclose offence for the regulated sector, with a defence for staff who lacked both suspicion and employer-provided training.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Recognising Unusual and Suspicious Transactions (MLR Regulation 24)
programs.why: The regulation 24 training must teach staff to recognise transactions and situations that may involve money laundering or terrorist financing. FCA guidance expects the content to reflect the bank's own risks and roles and to be tested, so frontline red-flag training is a direct legal requirement rather than optional awareness.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Training must cover how to recognise and deal with potentially suspicious transactions.

references.title: FCG 2 Financial crime systems and controls
references.note: Good practice includes role-tailored training with testing.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Transaction Monitoring and Alert Handling
programs.why: Banks must monitor relationships and transactions and have systems and controls proportionate to their financial crime risk under SYSC 6.3. Alert investigators need specialist skills to meet the competent employees rule and regulation 21 screening, but no specific monitoring course is prescribed.

references.title: SYSC 6.3 Financial crime
references.note: Requires systems and controls to identify, assess, monitor and manage money laundering risk.

references.title: SYSC 5.1 Skills, knowledge and expertise
references.note: Competent employees rule: staff must have the skills, knowledge and expertise their responsibilities require.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Correspondent Relationships EDD (MLR 2017)
programs.why: Correspondent relationships involving the execution of payments with respondent institutions from a third country attract mandatory enhanced due diligence and senior management approval under regulation 34. The 2026 amendments add a parallel regulation 34A from February 2027, but it applies to cryptoasset exchange and custodian wallet providers, not to banks. Staff managing these relationships need specialist knowledge; no separate training rule exists.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Enhanced measures for payment correspondent relationships with third-country respondents, including understanding the respondent's controls and senior management approval.

references.title: The Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Regulations 2026
references.note: Inserts regulation 34A from 1 February 2027: similar correspondent EDD duties for cryptoasset exchange and custodian wallet providers only; banks remain under regulation 34.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Risk-Based Approach and Firm-Wide Risk Assessment (MLR 2017)
programs.why: Banks must carry out and document a firm-wide ML/TF risk assessment and base their policies, controls and procedures on it; regulation 24 itself is applied in proportion to the size, nature and risk of the business. Staff who own risk assessments need to understand the risk-based approach, but no separate course is required.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Firm-wide risk assessment and the policies, controls and procedures that must follow from it.

programs.title: United Kingdom | AML Record-Keeping (MLR 2017)
programs.why: The Regulations require CDD and transaction records to be kept for set periods and, under regulation 24, a written record of training measures. Staff handling customer files must understand retention and deletion rules, which also interact with data protection law; no specific record-keeping course is prescribed.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Record-keeping duties for due diligence documents and transaction records.

programs.title: United Kingdom | AML for Frontline and Branch Staff (MLR Regulation 24)
programs.why: Frontline staff are relevant employees because they can help identify and prevent money laundering, so regulation 24 training applies to them directly. FCA guidance treats role-tailored financial crime training before customer contact as good practice and criticises firms that train only at induction or never test understanding.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Defines relevant employees by reference to their role in compliance or in detecting and preventing ML/TF.

references.title: FCG 2 Financial crime systems and controls
references.note: Good practice: customer-facing joiners get role-specific financial crime training before serving customers.

programs.title: United Kingdom | AML Accountability for Senior Management and the MLRO
programs.why: The Regulations require a board member or senior manager to be responsible for compliance, and SYSC 6.3 requires an MLRO with sufficient authority; under the SM&CR this is a senior management function. These individuals must be competent and their skills are assessed through screening and fitness checks, but no specific course is prescribed.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Board-level compliance officer, nominated officer, and screening of relevant employees' skills, knowledge and integrity.

references.title: SYSC 6.3 Financial crime
references.note: Allocation of AML oversight responsibility and the MLRO role.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Bribery Act 2010 Adequate Procedures
audience: Staff handling gifts, hospitality and intermediaries
programs.why: Section 7 of the Bribery Act makes a company liable for failing to prevent bribery by associated persons unless it had adequate procedures. The Ministry of Justice guidance names communication including training as one of six principles and suggests induction training plus continuing, monitored training. The FCA also expects banks to counter bribery risk through financial crime systems and controls.

references.title: Bribery Act 2010 guidance
references.note: Statutory guidance under section 9 on adequate procedures; training should be proportionate, start at induction and be continuous.

references.title: FCG 1 Introduction
references.note: The Financial Crime Guide covers bribery and corruption systems and controls for firms.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Failure to Prevent Fraud (ECCTA 2023) and APP Scams
programs.why: Since 1 September 2025, large organisations commit an offence under section 199 of the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 if an associated person commits fraud for their benefit, unless reasonable prevention procedures were in place. Home Office guidance lists communication including training among its six principles. Banks also reimburse APP scam victims under the PSR requirement, which raises the value of frontline fraud awareness.

references.title: Offence of 'failure to prevent fraud' introduced by ECCTA
references.note: Guidance on reasonable procedures, including communication and training, for the offence in force from 1 September 2025.

references.title: PS23/4 Fighting authorised push payment scams: final decision
references.note: Sets the mandatory reimbursement requirement for APP scams over Faster Payments.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Board Responsibilities under the Consumer Duty and SM&CR
programs.why: The board must at least annually review and approve a report on customer outcomes and confirm the bank complies with the Consumer Duty, and directors in senior management functions are approved and held to the Senior Manager Conduct Rules. Directors therefore need enough knowledge to challenge management; the annual frequency reflects the board review cycle, not a prescribed course.

references.title: PRIN 2A.2 Cross-cutting obligations (PRIN 2A The Consumer Duty)
references.note: Governing body must review and approve an outcomes report at least yearly and agree actions.

references.title: Consumer Duty board reports: good practice and areas for improvement
references.note: FCA observations on how boards use outcome data and challenge management.

references.title: FG22/5 Final non-Handbook Guidance for firms on the Consumer Duty
references.note: The governing body should review and approve the firm's assessment of whether it delivers good outcomes, and agree actions, at least annually.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Senior Managers Regime and Duty of Responsibility
programs.why: Under the SM&CR, senior managers are pre-approved, hold documented responsibilities and are subject to the duty of responsibility and Senior Manager Conduct Rules. The 2026 Phase 1 review (PS26/6) streamlined parts of the regime and Phase 2 (CP26/37) proposes further cuts, so senior managers need current knowledge of their accountability; no separate training is prescribed for them.

references.title: PS26/6: Senior Managers and Certification Regime review
references.note: Phase 1 changes, mostly effective 24 April 2026, with some later dates.

references.title: FCA and PRA confirm changes to streamline senior manager accountability and boost growth
references.note: Joint FCA/PRA announcement of the final Phase 1 SM&CR changes.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Fitness and Propriety and the Certification Regime
programs.why: Banks must assess the fitness and propriety of senior managers and certified staff, and screen relevant employees' skills and integrity under the Money Laundering Regulations. Competence is part of the test, but no course is prescribed. FCA CP26/37 (October 2026) proposes removing the Certification Regime, so this area may change in 2027.

references.title: CP26/37: Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SM&CR) Review: Phase 2
references.note: Consultation proposing removal of the Certification Regime and the Directory; closes January 2027.

references.title: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
references.note: Screening of relevant employees' skills, knowledge, conduct and integrity before and during appointment.

programs.title: United Kingdom | FCA/PRA Conduct Rules Training (COCON)
programs.why: Section 64B of FSMA and COCON 2.3 require banks to tell everyone subject to the Conduct Rules which rules apply to them and to take all reasonable steps, expressly including suitable training, to make sure they understand them. The FCA expects role-relevant, scenario-based training built into onboarding, reinforced regularly, overseen by the responsible senior manager and assessed for effectiveness. Since September 2026, COCON 4.3 also gives guidance on harassment as a Conduct Rule breach. CP26/37 proposes replacing the duty with a notification rule.

references.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, section 64B
references.note: Authorised persons must notify staff of the conduct rules that apply to them and take all reasonable steps, including suitable training, so they understand them.

references.title: FCA Handbook - COCON 2 Individual conduct rules
references.note: Notification and training duty so that staff understand how the Conduct Rules apply to them.

references.title: Conduct Rules
references.note: FCA expectations on line-manager involvement, onboarding, regular reinforcement and measuring training effectiveness.

references.title: CP26/37: Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SM&CR) Review: Phase 2
references.note: Proposes not replicating the statutory training duty (to be removed by legislation) and instead requiring firms to notify staff of the rules and the consequences of breach; not yet in force.

programs.title: United Kingdom | FCA Whistleblowing Arrangements Training (SYSC 18)
programs.why: SYSC 18.3 requires banks to give appropriate training to three groups: all UK-based staff (how to raise concerns and the protections available), managers of UK-based staff wherever they are based (recognising and handling disclosures and protecting confidentiality) and those who operate the arrangements. The FCA's review of banks found training was a key weakness, with most firms not differentiating training for managers and investigators.

references.title: SYSC 18.3 Internal arrangements
references.note: Internal whistleblowing arrangements must include appropriate training for staff, managers and those running the arrangements.

references.title: Retail and Wholesale Banking: review of firms' whistleblowing arrangements
references.note: Restates the duty to train UK staff, their managers and those running the arrangements; found training detail and annual board reporting the main weaknesses, with most firms not differentiating training by role.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Personal Regulatory Accountability under the SM&CR
programs.why: The SM&CR makes individuals personally answerable to the FCA and PRA through the Conduct Rules, the duty of responsibility and fitness checks. Individuals need to understand how their own accountability works and how it may change following the 2026 reviews; the express training duty sits in COCON 2.3 (program 38), so this module is a competence expectation.

references.title: FCA Handbook - COCON 2 Individual conduct rules
references.note: Individual and Senior Manager Conduct Rules that create personal accountability.

references.title: PS26/6: Senior Managers and Certification Regime review
references.note: Phase 1 changes to the regime in 2026.

programs.title: United Kingdom | FCA Consumer Duty (PRIN 2A)
programs.why: The Consumer Duty requires banks to act in good faith, avoid foreseeable harm and support retail customers' financial objectives, and to embed the Duty in strategy, governance, leadership and people policies. FCA reviews found some firms did not train staff well enough for complex customer conversations and expect training to an appropriate level. Staff knowledge is therefore needed, but the Duty does not prescribe a course.

references.title: PRIN 2A.2 Cross-cutting obligations
references.note: Cross-cutting obligations, and a requirement to reflect the Duty in people policies and governance.

references.title: FG22/5 Final non-Handbook Guidance for firms on the Consumer Duty
references.note: FCA guidance on applying the Duty, including reflecting good outcomes in strategy, governance, leadership and people policies.

references.title: Consumer Duty implementation: good practice and areas for improvement
references.note: Notes firms not training staff well enough for complex customer conversations and expects training to an appropriate level to support good outcomes.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Creditworthiness and Affordability (CONC 5.2A)
programs.why: Before entering a regulated credit agreement a bank must carry out a reasonable creditworthiness assessment covering both credit risk and affordability for the customer, without relying on security. Underwriters must be competent to apply these rules, but no separate training requirement is set in CONC.

references.title: FCA 2018/44 Consumer Credit (Creditworthiness) Instrument 2018
references.note: Introduced the detailed creditworthiness and affordability rules for consumer credit.

programs.title: United Kingdom | FCA Complaints Handling (DISP 1)
programs.why: DISP 1.3 requires effective and transparent complaint procedures, root-cause analysis and a senior individual responsible for oversight. Its guidance expects lessons from Financial Ombudsman decisions and regulator guidance to be passed to complaint-handling staff, including through training. The guidance status means this is a competence expectation rather than a prescribed course.

references.title: DISP 1.3 Complaints handling rules
references.note: Complaint procedures, root-cause analysis and guidance on feeding ombudsman decisions into staff training.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Vulnerable Customers (FCA FG21/1)
programs.why: FCA guidance expects all relevant staff to understand how their role affects vulnerable customers and frontline staff to have the skills to recognise and respond to vulnerability, with support proportionate to the firm. Under the Consumer Duty, vulnerable customers should get outcomes as good as other customers. The FCA's 2025 review of retail banks found training and competency issues contributed to staff not following processes.

references.title: FG21/1 Guidance for firms on the fair treatment of vulnerable customers
references.note: Sets expectations on staff skills and capability to identify and respond to vulnerability.

references.title: Retail banks' treatment of customers in vulnerable circumstances multi-firm review
references.note: Found training and competency issues contributing to staff not following processes.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Customer Data Confidentiality (UK GDPR)
programs.why: Banks must protect customer personal data under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. The ICO's accountability framework expects all-staff training with induction and refresher elements, and treats awareness and training as evidence that policies are actually followed. The law does not prescribe a course for all staff, so this is a competence expectation.

references.title: Training and awareness (Accountability Framework)
references.note: ICO expectations for induction, refresher and role-specific data protection training.

references.title: Guide to accountability and governance
references.note: Explains that organisations must be able to show policies are implemented, including through training.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Arrears, Default and Recovery (CONC 7)
programs.why: CONC 7 requires banks to treat customers in or near arrears with forbearance and due consideration, to agree sustainable repayment plans and to avoid disproportionate action or pressure. Collections staff need this knowledge to meet the competent employees rule and the Consumer Duty, but no separate course is required.

references.title: FCA Handbook - CONC 7 Arrears, default and recovery (including repossessions)
references.note: Forbearance, sustainable arrangements and fair treatment of customers in financial difficulty.

programs.title: United Kingdom | FCA Training and Competence Regime (TC) for Advisers
programs.why: The TC sourcebook applies to staff doing the retail activities listed in TC Appendix 1. They must be supervised until assessed as competent, must hold an appropriate qualification where required (some before starting), and must have their competence reviewed regularly. All other staff fall under the general competent employees rule in SYSC 5.1.

references.title: FCA Handbook - TC 2.1 Assessing and maintaining competence
references.note: Competence assessment, supervision, appropriate qualifications and regular review for TC activities.

references.title: Training and competence
references.note: FCA overview of the competent employees rule and the TC qualification requirements.

references.title: FCA Handbook - SYSC 5.1 Skills, knowledge and expertise
references.note: High-level competent employees rule for all staff.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Information Security Awareness (UK GDPR Security Principle)
programs.why: UK GDPR requires appropriate technical and organisational security measures. ICO guidance treats staff awareness as part of those measures. Banks also need secure systems to meet PRA and FCA systems-and-controls rules. Staff awareness is therefore expected, though no specific course is prescribed.

references.title: A guide to data security
references.note: ICO guidance on the security principle, including organisational measures such as staff awareness.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Cyber Resilience Awareness (PRA/FCA Operational Resilience)
programs.why: PRA and FCA operational resilience rules require banks to stay within impact tolerances for important business services in severe but plausible scenarios, including cyber attacks. PRA priorities for 2026 stress recovery from cyber incidents. Staff awareness supports these controls, but no cyber training is prescribed.

references.title: PS6/21 Operational resilience: Impact tolerances for important business services
references.note: PRA operational resilience rules; firms had to be able to remain within impact tolerances by 31 March 2025.

references.title: Operational resilience
references.note: FCA operational resilience expectations for firms.

programs.title: United Kingdom | UK GDPR, DPA 2018 and Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
programs.why: Where a bank has a data protection officer, UK GDPR Article 39 makes awareness-raising and training of processing staff part of the DPO's tasks, and the ICO expects induction and refresher training. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 is now fully in force, including a duty from 19 June 2026 to handle data protection complaints. Training is expected, but no all-staff course is set by statute.

references.title: United Kingdom General Data Protection Regulation, Article 39
references.note: DPO tasks include monitoring compliance, including awareness-raising and training of staff involved in processing.

references.title: Data protection officers
references.note: ICO guidance on DPO duties, including training.

references.title: New data protection complaints law now in force
references.note: Organisations must offer a route to complain, acknowledge within 30 days, investigate and report the outcome.

references.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 164A
references.note: Controllers must make it easy to complain about data protection infringements, acknowledge within 30 days and respond and report the outcome without undue delay; inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Operational Incident Reporting (FCA PS26/2, PRA PS7/26)
programs.why: From 18 March 2027 a single FCA/PRA/Bank of England regime will require operational incidents to be reported through one portal on common timelines and material third-party arrangements to be reported. Staff who detect and escalate incidents must recognise what is reportable; the rules set reporting duties, not training.

references.title: PS26/2: Operational incident and third party reporting
references.note: Final rules on incident and third-party reporting applying from 18 March 2027.

references.title: SS1/26
references.note: PRA supervisory statement on operational incident reporting, effective 18 March 2027.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Personal Data Breach Management (UK GDPR and ICO)
programs.why: UK GDPR requires notifiable personal data breaches to be reported to the ICO without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, and high-risk breaches to be told to affected individuals. The ICO audit framework expects staff to be trained to recognise and escalate breaches quickly. The training element is guidance, so this is a competence expectation.

references.title: Training (Personal data breach management toolkit)
references.note: ICO expectation that staff are trained to identify and report personal data breaches.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Operational Resilience (PRA SS1/21 and FCA SYSC 15A)
programs.why: Banks must identify important business services, set impact tolerances, map and test them and, since 31 March 2025, be able to remain within tolerance in severe but plausible scenarios. The PRA now expects better resilience testing. Staff and management who run this framework must understand it, but no training is prescribed.

references.title: PS6/21 Operational resilience: Impact tolerances for important business services
references.note: Rules and supervisory statement SS1/21; compliance deadline 31 March 2025.

references.title: Operational resilience
references.note: FCA operational resilience requirements and expectations.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Outsourcing and Third-Party Risk (PRA SS2/21)
programs.why: PRA SS2/21 sets expectations for managing outsourcing and third-party risk, updated in March 2026 alongside new third-party reporting rules effective 18 March 2027. Staff who contract with and oversee suppliers need to know the requirements; no specific training is prescribed.

references.title: Supervisory Statement SS2/21 Outsourcing and third party risk management (March 2026 update)
references.note: Updated PRA expectations on outsourcing and third-party risk.

references.title: Reporting material third party arrangements
references.note: FCA guidance on the new register submission for material third-party arrangements.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Bullying and Harassment as Conduct Rule Breaches (COCON 4.3)
programs.why: FCA rules and guidance in force from 1 September 2026 make clear that work-related bullying, harassment and violence towards colleagues can breach the Conduct Rules and affect fitness and propriety. Because banks must already train staff on the Conduct Rules, this content belongs in conduct training, but no separate harassment course is prescribed by the FCA.

references.title: FCA Handbook - COCON 4.3 Specific guidance on harassment
references.note: Guidance on when bullying or harassment breaches Individual Conduct Rules 1 or 2.

references.title: PS25/23: Tackling non-financial misconduct in financial services
references.note: Policy statement introducing the non-financial misconduct rules and guidance.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Preventing Sexual Harassment (Equality Act 2010 s.40A)
programs.why: Employers have had a duty since October 2024 to take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of their workers. From 30 October 2026 the Employment Rights Act 2025 raises this to all reasonable steps and adds liability for third-party harassment. The EHRC technical guidance gives manager training and refresher training for all staff as examples of reasonable steps, though the statute does not name training.

references.title: Equality Act 2010, section 40A
references.note: Employers must take all reasonable steps (the word 'all' added from 30 October 2026) to prevent sexual harassment of their employees in the course of employment.

references.title: Sexual harassment and harassment at work: technical guidance
references.note: Explains the preventative duty and lists training among reasonable steps.

references.title: Employment Rights Act 2025 (protection from harassment and discrimination)
references.note: Section 20 adds 'all' to the s.40A duty, s.21 makes employers liable for third-party harassment of employees unless they took all reasonable steps, and s.22 allows regulations to specify reasonable steps; all in force 30 October 2026.

references.title: The Employment Rights Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026
references.note: Brings the strengthened harassment provisions into force.

programs.title: United Kingdom | Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 Employer Training Duty
programs.why: Section 2(2)(c) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 requires employers, so far as reasonably practicable, to provide the information, instruction, training and supervision needed for employees' health and safety. HSE guidance points to new recruits and people changing jobs as needing particular attention, which covers branch, office and home-working staff.

references.title: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, section 2
references.note: Employer must provide necessary information, instruction, training and supervision for health and safety.

references.title: Provide information, training and supervision: Overview
references.note: HSE guidance on delivering health and safety training, including for new recruits.

programs.title: United Kingdom | FATCA Due Diligence and Reporting to HMRC
programs.why: UK banks are reporting financial institutions under the International Tax Compliance Regulations 2015 and must identify US reportable accounts and report them to HMRC. From the 2025 amendments, a single mandatory AEOI registration covers both FATCA and CRS. Staff collecting self-certifications must understand these rules, but no training duty is set.

references.title: The International Tax Compliance (Amendment) Regulations 2025
references.note: Adds mandatory registration and penalties covering FATCA and CRS institutions.

programs.title: United Kingdom | CRS 2.0 Due Diligence and Reporting (HMRC)
programs.why: The amended CRS rules apply from 1 January 2026, with first reports under them due in 2027, new penalties and expanded scope. Banks must collect valid self-certifications and report reportable accounts to HMRC. Staff need current knowledge of these due diligence steps, though no training obligation applies.

references.title: The International Tax Compliance (Amendment) Regulations 2025
references.note: Implements the amended Common Reporting Standard in UK law from 1 January 2026.

references.title: IEIM400080 - Background: Common Reporting Standard
references.note: HMRC manual explaining the CRS framework for UK financial institutions.

notes: The Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/621) were made on 9 June 2026; most provisions took effect on 30 June 2026 (including replacing 'high-risk third country' with FATF call-for-action countries), a new regulation 34A on correspondent EDD for cryptoasset firms applies from 1 February 2027, and some cryptoasset change-of-control rules follow on 25 October 2027. Regulation 24 (training) is not amended.

FCA CP26/37 (October 2026, closing January 2027) proposes removing the Certification Regime and replacing the COCON training requirement with a notification duty. Until final rules are made, COCON 2.3 training still applies.
SM&CR Phase 1 changes (FCA PS26/6 and PRA PS12/26) took effect mostly from 24 April 2026, with further changes in July 2026.
FCA non-financial misconduct rules and COCON 4.3 harassment guidance took effect on 1 September 2026.
The Employment Rights Act 2025 strengthened the sexual harassment prevention duty to 'all reasonable steps' and added third-party harassment liability from 30 October 2026.
The ECCTA 2023 failure to prevent fraud offence has applied to large organisations since 1 September 2025.
The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 is fully in force; the duty to handle data protection complaints applies from 19 June 2026.
New single FCA/PRA/Bank of England operational incident and third-party reporting rules (FCA PS26/2, PRA PS7/26) apply from 18 March 2027.

CRS 2.0 changes apply from 1 January 2026, with a single mandatory AEOI registration for FATCA and CRS. The PSR is being consolidated into the FCA, which may change who supervises APP scam reimbursement.
